findings.title: Findings converge on the "every live non-daemon thread is a survivor" signal
findings.why_it_matters: D3's thread rule treats any non-daemon thread other than the main thread that is still alive inside `main()` after the bound as work that holds the process. Three findings from both critics hit that one inference from different directions. Idle AnyIO workers are alive inside `main()` on almost every exit (Finding 2). The default executor's own `_do_shutdown` helper thread stays alive whenever a worker is stuck (Finding 4). A user app's own thread gets cut by `os._exit` and exits 0 (Finding 9). Each proposes its own patch: a name allowlist, a target filter, a user-versus-framework split. Taken together, they ask whether "any live non-daemon thread, judged inside `main()`" is the right signal at all. Should the thread side of D3 be re-evaluated as a whole rather than patched three times? That includes asking whether it is worth having, or whether some of these cases are limitations to accept and document.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate D3's thread survivor signal before addressing Findings 2, 4 and 9 individually. Open questions: which threads count as work the framework left behind; whether the thread check belongs inside `main()` or after `asyncio.run()` has stopped its own workers; whether user-owned threads are in scope at all; whether any of these cases is better accepted and documented.
findings.chosen: re-evaluated: H, HA's split (interruptible default executor + bounded threading._shutdown join)

findings.title: The thread check reports idle AnyIO workers as survivors on a clean exit
findings.why_it_matters: On a clean shutdown, D3 turns any live non-daemon thread into one ERROR plus `os._exit`, which skips atexit handlers and finalizers. Starlette's `StaticFiles` and `FileResponse` run file I/O through `anyio.to_thread.run_sync`, whose worker threads are non-daemon. They are stopped only when the root task (`asyncio.run`'s main task, wrapping `main()`) finishes, which is after D3's check. Synthesis verification makes this worse than the critic's "~10s" window. AnyIO's 10s idle pruning only runs when a later `run_sync` call arrives, and `WorkerThread.run` blocks on `queue.get()` with no timeout. So at least one worker stays alive for the rest of the process once the UI has served any file. Every clean `hassette run` exit after someone opened the UI would log a false ERROR and hard-exit.
findings.recommended: C: Move the thread half of the check to after `asyncio.run()` returns (where AnyIO and the default executor have already stopped their workers), as HA does, and keep the task half inside `main()`.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: The exit check's bound depends on a responsive loop, and on Python 3.11 the bounded executor shutdown blocks the loop outright
findings.why_it_matters: Every step of D3's rule runs as a coroutine on the event loop it is meant to rescue. Anything that blocks the loop during the check means the bound never fires, so no ERROR is logged and no `os._exit` runs, and the process holds until the supervisor kill. Synthesis verification found a concrete, non-rare trigger that the ledger's Assumed section gets wrong. CPython 3.11's `shutdown_default_executor()` ends in `finally: thread.join()` with no timeout. So bounding it with `wait_for`, as the Assumed bullet ("the check bounds it itself") implies, cancels the `await` and then blocks the loop thread synchronously until the stuck worker returns. That is exactly the case the check exists for. Separately, after the default executor is shut down, `asyncio.to_thread` can't be used to wait on threads. The ledger doesn't say whether the thread wait is an `asyncio.sleep` poll or a blocking `Thread.join`. A blocking join would starve the cancelled tasks still finishing, and that produces false survivors. A cancelled task whose cleanup makes a sync blocking call freezes the loop the same way on every version.
findings.recommended: A: State in D3 that the thread wait is an `asyncio.sleep` poll, and that the default-executor shutdown is never cancelled. On 3.12+ pass its `timeout`. On 3.11 start it without awaiting it under a cancelling timeout. Correct the Assumed bullet. Accept a loop frozen by sync cleanup as a documented gap.
findings.chosen: A: State in D3 that the thread wait is an `asyncio.sleep` poll, and that the default-executor shutdown is never cancelled

findings.title: The default executor's shutdown helper thread is itself reported as a survivor
findings.why_it_matters: `loop.shutdown_default_executor()` starts a non-daemon helper thread that runs `executor.shutdown(wait=True)`. When a worker is stuck, that helper stays alive. Synthesis verification shows this happens on 3.12+ too, where the `timeout` path warns and returns but leaves the helper thread running. So the one survivor ERROR names `Thread-N (_do_shutdown)` next to the real culprit, which is noise in the line an operator reads at 2am. On 3.11, when the helper finally finishes, it posts `future.set_result` to a cancelled future or a closed loop, which prints a stray traceback. After the call, `_executor_shutdown_called` is set, so any later `to_thread` raises `RuntimeError`. Only tasks that already survived the task wait can hit that.
findings.recommended: A: Exclude the `_do_shutdown` helper from the survivor set, and state in D3 that a stuck default-executor worker is named by its own thread.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Whether a task that finishes cancellation within the bound logs an ERROR is not pinned
findings.why_it_matters: D3's table row for "a framework task that outlives a clean shutdown" can be read as the ERROR firing for any cancelled task, not only a survivor. Read that way, a lingering library task (uvicorn, a websocket heartbeat) would turn every clean exit into an ERROR. D4 asserts that "a clean exit's tasks finish in one loop turn" without evidence. Today `asyncio.run` cancels leftovers silently, so nobody has observed what is alive at that point.
findings.chosen: In D3, add to the Rule: "A task that finishes within the bound after being cancelled is not a survivor and logs nothing above DEBUG." Add to "Behavior to pin": "a task that takes about 1s to finish its cancellation exits 0 with no ERROR."

findings.title: The harness-side successor to the `force_terminated_work == ()` guards is unstated
findings.why_it_matters: `test_bus_death.py:41` asserts `hassette.force_terminated_work == ()` as a "no send blocked teardown into a force-termination" guard. `test_core_coverage.py:368,485,539` assert names in or out of the list, and `test_main.py` mocks it. The live check never runs in the harness, so these guards need a successor on the outcome. Otherwise they get rewritten loosely during the migration of about 20 test files, or deleted.
findings.chosen: Add to D3's "Behavior to pin": "In the harness, the root's `shutdown_outcome.result is not ShutdownResult.INCOMPLETE` replaces `force_terminated_work == ()` (a force-terminated descendant merges up as INCOMPLETE). Tests that asserted a specific name assert the stage's ERROR log instead."

findings.title: `RestartRefusedError.report` and `describe_left_running()`'s `force_terminated` flag are left unresolved
findings.why_it_matters: `RestartRefusedError` is a `FatalError` embedders catch, and it exposes `resource_name` and `report` typed as `TeardownReport`. D5 renames the type but not the attribute. The build would make that call silently. `describe_left_running()` takes a separate `force_terminated: bool` next to the report. Under D2 the reason string already says what forced the teardown, so the flag becomes a second source for "this was force-terminated".
findings.recommended: A: Rename the attribute to `outcome`, add it to D5's migration note, and drop `describe_left_running()`'s `force_terminated` parameter in favor of the outcome's reason.
findings.chosen: A: Rename the attribute to `outcome`, add it to D5's migration note, and drop `describe_left_running()`'s `force_terminated` parameter in favor of the outcome's reason

findings.title: Survivor thread names are unactionable
findings.why_it_matters: Leaked default-executor work shows up as `asyncio_0` or `Thread-12`, which tells an operator nothing about what is stuck. The repo already has a helper that logs a surviving thread's name and current stack, mirroring HA's, and D3 doesn't say to reuse it.
findings.chosen: In D3's Rule, after "Survivors get one ERROR naming every surviving task and thread", add: "and each surviving thread's stack is logged through the existing `_log_thread_running_at_shutdown()` (`task_bucket/interruptible_executor.py`)."

findings.title: A user app's non-daemon thread is cut by `os._exit` after 5s, with exit 0
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: user apps are arbitrary Python written against a framework and may start a plain `threading.Thread` for a worker or a device client. Today such a thread holds the interpreter at exit. Under D3 it gets 5s after `on_shutdown`, then `os._exit` skips atexit handlers, buffered output and user cleanup, and the exit code is 0, so a supervisor logs a success. D3's table lists "a thread a user started: Caught" only as a win. One ERROR names the thread, so the cut is not silent, but nothing in the exit code or the app docs tells the user this happens.
findings.recommended: C: Accept as a known limitation: a user's non-daemon thread still running 5s after shutdown is cut by `os._exit`, skipping atexit, with exit 0 and one ERROR naming it. Record it in D3's `accepting` clause and in the app lifecycle docs ("join your threads in `on_shutdown`").
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: The survivor ERROR can be lost to the logging queue before `os._exit`
findings.why_it_matters: `LoggingService.on_shutdown` is the only place the `QueueHandler` comes off and the sync stream handler goes back on. If the stop stage walked away from LoggingService (the stuck-shutdown case the check exists for), the survivor ERROR goes into the queue. `logging.shutdown()` doesn't drain a `QueueHandler`, and `os._exit` races the daemon listener thread, so the one line that matters can vanish. The same race exists today in `exit_now_if_work_force_terminated`, and the redesign rewrites that function without closing it.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: if LoggingService's shutdown was abandoned, the survivor ERROR may be lost to the logging queue before `os._exit`.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: if LoggingService's shutdown was abandoned, the survivor ERROR may be lost to the logging queue before `os._exit`.

findings.title: The check waits on the snapshot before recording anything, so a kill leaves no evidence
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: HAOS add-on users on slow storage (SD card or eMMC) with a large telemetry DB, where a snapshot copy over 10s is plausible. D4's grace math holds only at defaults. The snapshot copy is unbounded by design, `total_shutdown_timeout_seconds` is a user field with only a lower bound, and the root's post-children work sits outside every budget. D4 ratified losing the survivor ERROR to the kill. The open point is ordering. The task and thread scan doesn't need to wait for the snapshot, and only the executor shutdown does. Yet D3 waits for the snapshot before anything is recorded.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a snapshot slower than about 10s plus a survivor lets the supervisor's kill land with no record of the survivors. This is already D4's accepting clause.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a snapshot slower than about 10s plus a survivor lets the supervisor's kill land with no record of the survivors. This is already D4's accepting clause.

findings.title: "First reason at the worst rank" is an arrival-order artifact among siblings
findings.why_it_matters: D2 keeps the first reason recorded at the merged rank. When several siblings in one wave end INCOMPLETE, "first" is their position in the merged list, not which one caused the trouble, and the needs-restart reason shows that one. Synthesis verification narrows the critic's other example. When a forced-terminal report is already stored, the coordinator returns it and cancels the body (`lifecycle.py:679-686`), so a later "body raised" reason is never produced. "Forced terminal" is then the true cause, and that path masks nothing.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: when several siblings end INCOMPLETE, the reason names the first in child order, and the others are in the logs.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: when several siblings end INCOMPLETE, the reason names the first in child order, and the others are in the logs.

findings.title: A pending initializer in `still_running` surfaces an internal task label
findings.why_it_matters: D1 moves a pending initializer into `still_running` under its task name, `resource:initialize:<unique_name>`. The guard is unaffected, and the name includes the resource, so dedupe is safe. But `describe_left_running()` would print "work is still running: resource:initialize:App.x", and the wire's `NeedsRestart.pending_tasks` would carry a label shaped differently from TaskBucket task names.
findings.chosen: Side A: Keep the raw task name

findings.title: No test route for the survivor path
findings.why_it_matters: `os._exit` can't be asserted in-process, and the executor-shutdown behavior differs between 3.11 and 3.12+ (Findings 3 and 4). If the five "Behavior to pin" bullets are tested against a mocked `os._exit`, they will pass while missing the loop freeze and the helper thread. A subprocess pattern already exists, and CI runs the system suite on all four supported Pythons.
findings.chosen: Side A: Subprocess system test

findings.title: Exit policy is spread over five places that must agree
The in-loop executor shutdown blocks the loop
The exit watchdog can block in logging or die before it reaches `os._exit`
findings.why_it_matters: D3 ratifies the rule "when exit is stuck past the budget, hassette guarantees the process ends", and the watchdog is the only thing behind that guarantee. `watch()` has no `try/finally`. Before `os._exit` it calls `LOGGER.error`, then `log_thread_running_at_shutdown()` for every thread, then `hard_exit()`, which runs `logging.shutdown()` before `os._exit`. After LoggingService shuts down, the synchronous `StreamHandler` on `sys.stdout` is back in place (`logging_service.py:163-166`), so every one of those calls is a blocking stdout write under the handler's lock.
findings.recommended: C: Accept as a known limitation: when a stuck exit coincides with a blocked log sink, the watchdog can block in logging, and the supervisor's kill ends the process
findings.chosen: C: Accept as a known limitation

findings.title: The real-process exit pins use a fake core, so the AnyIO assumption is unproven in hassette
findings.why_it_matters: D3's Assumed section says AnyIO stopping its idle workers before the deadline "is a library detail, so D3's real-exit pin is what proves it in hassette." The pin doesn't prove that. `exit_child.py` swaps `server.create_core` for a `SimpleNamespace` and `server.serve` for a scripted coroutine, and its `idle_anyio` scenario calls `anyio.to_thread.run_sync` from that coroutine, not through FastAPI/Starlette under uvicorn. The one existing real-process exit test, `test_single_signal_exits_promptly_on_healthy_instance`, runs a real `hassette run` but checks only the return code and a 10s limit. It reads stdout without inspecting it, and the watchdog fires at about 6s with exit code 0. So a real exit that ends by the watchdog, or by the task half's hard exit, still passes.
findings.recommended: A: Extend `test_single_signal_exits_promptly_on_healthy_instance` to drive an AnyIO-thread request first and assert that neither exit ERROR appears in the captured stdout
findings.chosen: A: Extend the existing real-process test

findings.title: A hard exit with surviving work exits with the clean-stop code
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a deployment where apps have legitimate slow shutdown work that is not tracked by a TaskBucket. `exit_after_run` and the watchdog judge "stuck" by elapsed time alone (5s, then 6s), and both hard exits use the mapped code, which is 0 after a clean stop. A supervisor, a systemd unit or the add-on's s6 script can't tell a clean exit from one cut off mid-flush. The only signal is an ERROR line. The trigger is also wider than the old one: the old hard exit needed a recorded force-termination, while the new one fires on any task alive at 5s, including user-app tasks the framework never recorded, and on any slow finalization past about 6s (senior-engineer's Finding 7). The budget has no override.
findings.chosen: Side B: distinct exit code (70, EX_SOFTWARE)
findings.choice_reason: Asked whether peers use a distinct code; systemd marks a stop past TimeoutStopSec failed, HA keeps the requested code. Picked 70 over 124.

findings.title: The needs-restart text drops the reason unless the result is INCOMPLETE
findings.why_it_matters: D2 exists to replace the generic "evidence is incomplete" with the resource and step that caused it. `describe_left_running()` adds `outcome.reason` only when `result is INCOMPLETE`. A `TIMED_OUT` or `FAILED` outcome that also names `still_running` tasks is restart-unsafe (`shutdown_outcome.py:76`) and gets flagged, but its needs-restart reason and ERROR say only "stop timed out after Xs; work is still running: …" or "stopped, but work is still running: …". The hook or `cleanup()` that caused it isn't named. This combination is the one an operator most needs explained: a hook timed out or raised and left tasks behind. `RestartRefusedError` includes the reason, so the two surfaces disagree.
findings.chosen: In `describe_left_running()`, put `outcome.reason` in front whenever it is set, not only for `INCOMPLETE`. Update its docstring and the Build bullet at design.md:321 to match. Add a test for a `TIMED_OUT` outcome (and a `FAILED` one) that names `still_running` tasks, asserting the needs-restart reason contains the hook's reason.

findings.title: The PR's `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer must cover more than the three renames
findings.why_it_matters: The branch squash-merges, so the PR body's one `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer becomes the user's migration note (release-please keeps only the first footer). The PR doesn't exist yet. The `feat!:` commit's footer names only `TeardownReport`/`TeardownCause` → `ShutdownOutcome`/`ShutdownResult`, `teardown_report` → `shutdown_outcome`, and `RestartRefusedError.report` → `.outcome`. The diff also removes or changes:
findings.chosen: When `/mine-ship` writes the PR body, its single `BREAKING CHANGE:` paragraph lists: the three renames already in the commit footer; that `RestartRefusedError`'s message format changed, so callers should read `.outcome`; that `Hassette.force_terminated_work` and `record_force_terminated()` are removed; that `hassette.server.main()` is replaced by `create_core()`/`serve()`/`run()`; and the new `hassette run` exit behavior in one sentence (cancel remaining tasks, hard exit after 5s, a watchdog after 1s more that skips atexit handlers, exit code unchanged), with a pointer to the operating docs.

findings.title: Tasks created during the exit cancellation are neither cancelled nor named
findings.why_it_matters: `cancel_remaining_tasks` takes `asyncio.all_tasks()` once, cancels that list, and waits only on it. A task created by another task's cancellation cleanup (a `finally` that does `asyncio.create_task(flush())`) isn't in the list. Hassette restores the previous task factory when shutdown ends (`core.py:726-733`), so such a task is created without a sealed bucket rejecting it. `asyncio.run()`'s own cancel-and-gather then cancels it. If it ignores cancellation, only the watchdog ends the process, and the watchdog names threads, not tasks: the log shows the main thread blocked in a gather. D3's pin "a task survivor is named by the task half's ERROR, not only by the watchdog's thread list" doesn't hold for such a task.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a task created by another task's cancellation cleanup that then ignores cancellation is ended by the watchdog and shown only as the main thread's stack
findings.chosen: B: Accept

findings.title: A task that raises during the exit cancellation is logged only at DEBUG
findings.why_it_matters: `cancel_remaining_tasks` retrieves each finished task's exception and logs it at DEBUG, whether the task was cancelled cleanly or its cleanup raised a real error (for example a failed flush). On main, `asyncio.run()`'s `_cancel_all_tasks` reported a task that ended with an exception through the loop's exception handler at ERROR. Now that report is gone. The ledger pin "logs nothing above DEBUG" was written for a clean cancel. Tasks tracked by a TaskBucket still get the bucket's own "task crashed" ERROR from its done-callback. Only untracked tasks lose their signal: `PROTECT_TASK` tasks, and tasks created after Hassette restores the task factory.
findings.chosen: Side B: WARNING for non-cancel exceptions

findings.title: On a stalled loop the watchdog can fire before the task half names a survivor
findings.why_it_matters: The task half writes its ERROR only after `asyncio.wait(timeout=remaining)` returns. If a long synchronous callback stalls the loop right at the deadline, the watchdog thread fires at deadline + 1s on its own and exits with only the thread list. A surviving task is then never named, and the two hard exits can race, since nothing orders them. The pin uses a 0.3s margin and covers only an unloaded loop.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a loop stalled more than 1s at the deadline lets the watchdog exit first, so a surviving task shows up only as the main thread's stack
findings.chosen: B: Accept

findings.title: The wire docstring for `pending_tasks` promises a core-internal task-name format
findings.why_it_matters: `NeedsRestart.pending_tasks` in the released `hassette-wire` package now documents its entries as including `resource:initialize:<unique name>`. That format is a literal in core (`lifecycle.py:543`), and the core test pins the literal, not the wire docstring. If the literal changes, the wire's published description (and the regenerated OpenAPI/WS schema) goes stale without any check catching it. D1 ratified exposing the raw task name in the UI and the reason, so only the coupling of the docs is in question.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: the wire docstring names the `resource:initialize:` format and goes stale if `lifecycle.py`'s literal changes
findings.chosen: B: Accept

findings.title: The "TIMED_OUT only means a hook cut off" rule is enforced by an inline comment in one call site
